category: collected letters and theological notes (posthumous, edited)

date.note: The letters and notes were written from Tegel military prison in Berlin between 1943 and 1945, before Bonhoeffer's execution on 9 April 1945. They were edited posthumously by his friend Eberhard Bethge and first published in German as Widerstand und Ergebung in 1951. The unabridged critical English edition appeared as Letters and Papers from Prison in the Dietrich Bonhoeffer Works series (Fortress Press, 2010, DBWE volume 8), edited by John W. de Gruchy. The year 1951 marks the first German edition; the material dates from 1943-1945.

summary: Letters and Papers from Prison (Widerstand und Ergebung) is a collection of letters and theological notes written by the German Lutheran pastor and theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer from Tegel military prison in Berlin between 1943 and 1945, before his execution, and edited and published posthumously by his friend Eberhard Bethge. The correspondence with Bethge from 1944 contains the fragmentary late ideas for which the collection became known, among them a 'religionless Christianity,' a 'world come of age,' and a God who is 'pushed out of the world onto the cross'; these are presented as attributed late reflections rather than a finished system.
description:
Letters and Papers from Prison (German Widerstand und Ergebung, 'Resistance and Submission') is a posthumously assembled collection of the letters and theological notes that Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906-1945), a German Lutheran pastor and theologian of the Confessing Church, wrote during his imprisonment at the Tegel military prison in Berlin. Arrested in 1943 for his connection to the circle around the Abwehr that conspired against Hitler, he was held at Tegel from April 1943 and wrote, among family correspondence and personal reflections, a series of letters to his friend and former student Eberhard Bethge; he was later moved to other prisons and executed at the Flossenbuerg concentration camp on 9 April 1945. Bethge preserved the smuggled letters and edited them for publication; they first appeared in German as Widerstand und Ergebung in 1951, and the unabridged critical English edition was published as Letters and Papers from Prison in the Dietrich Bonhoeffer Works series (Fortress Press, 2010, volume 8), edited by John W. de Gruchy.

The theological interest of the collection centers on a group of letters to Bethge from 1944 in which Bonhoeffer sketched ideas he did not live to develop. He wrote of a 'world come of age' (a world that has become adult), which he described as a humanity that manages its life, knowledge, and morality without appeal to God as a working hypothesis, so that the God invoked to fill the gaps in human knowledge or to answer at the boundaries of life is steadily pushed back. Against a Christianity that would defend such a God of the gaps, he called for a 'religionless Christianity' or a 'nonreligious interpretation' of biblical concepts, one that would speak of God not at the edges of life but at its center and in this-worldly terms. In the same letters he set against the powerful God of religion the God of the Bible who 'is weak and powerless in the world,' the God who lets himself be 'pushed out of the world onto the cross,' so that it is precisely by weakness and suffering, not by power, that this God is with and helps human beings. He linked this to a 'this-worldly' (diesseitig) Christian existence, living fully in the world's tasks and sufferings.

These ideas are contained in private letters and jottings, are fragmentary and unsystematic, and were left unfinished at Bonhoeffer's death; their interpretation is much debated among later scholars and theologians. This entry presents 'religionless Christianity,' the 'world come of age,' and the God 'pushed out of the world onto the cross' as Bonhoeffer's attributed late reflections, not as a completed doctrine, and it records that the editor Eberhard Bethge preserved and arranged these fragments without systematizing them into a finished theology. Bonhoeffer's imprisonment, the composition of the letters between 1943 and 1945, his execution on 9 April 1945, and the posthumous editing and publication are recorded as matters of historical report, without endorsing or adjudicating the theological claims the letters contain.
